audit.evidence: `njodb` is a persistent, partitioned, concurrency-controlled, Node JSON object database. Data is written to the file system and distributed across multiple files that are protected by read and write locks. By default, all methods are asynchronous and use read/write streams to improve performance and reduce memory requirements (this should be particularly useful for large databases). ／ **Completely schemaless** - While the JSON data itself is schemaless, it is also the case that data is not siloed into tables, or forced into collections, so the entire database, from top to bottom, is schemaless, not just the data. For a user or application, this means that there is no need to know anything about the database structure, only what data is being sought. ／ **Concurrency-controlled** - File locks are used during read and write operations, ensuring data integrity can be maintained in a multi-user/multi-application environment. There are few, if any, existing solutions that are designed for such scenarios and that include this sort of data protection.

audit.evidence: Deploy-safe Django migrations for PostgreSQL. Destructive schema changes (dropping a column or table, tightening a column to NOT NULL, reshaping a column) ship in one pull request and one deploy, and old code keeps working while the new release rolls out. ／ Migrations run before new code rolls out, and old code keeps serving requests until the rollout ends. django-deferred-migrations splits every migration run into two phases around that rollout. Operations such as `DeferredRemoveField` update Django's state immediately, make the old schema tolerate the new code, and queue the physical `DROP` for a post-deploy step that runs once the old code is gone. Only the destructive SQL is deferred, never a whole migration, so later migrations never wait on unrun work. That is also what lets it work with django-linear-migrations, however many pull requests land in one app between deploys. A `check_deploy_safety` command catches unsafe operations in CI, `fix_deploy_safety` rewrites the mechanical cases, and every DDL statement runs with a short lock timeout and retry, so a migration never queues behind a long transaction and stalls the site.

identity.review: CamusDB 是一个用 C#/.NET 实现的分布式 SQL 数据库，底层为 Raft 复制的事务性键值存储，支持可序列化隔离、写时复制数据库分支、已删除对象恢复、时间旅行读取与查询结果缓存，通过 JSON/HTTP 或 gRPC 接口访问，并提供可编译为 WebAssembly 的浏览器演示环境。适合需要强一致性默认语义的 .NET 开发者；README 明示部分功能仍为 alpha，API 与存储格式可能在版本间变化。
highlights: 默认可序列化隔离，跨分区写入基于 Raft 共识与两阶段提交
支持数据库写时复制分支、DROP 对象保留期恢复与 AS OF SYSTEM TIME 时间旅行读取
SQL 引擎与存储节点运行于单一 .NET 进程，亦可编译为 WebAssembly 在浏览器运行
use_cases: 需要强一致性默认语义的分布式 SQL 数据存储
为 schema 迁移演练或每 PR 创建临时数据库克隆的分支场景
误删行或误操作数据后基于多版本历史读取恢复

audit.evidence: CamusDB is a SQL distributed database written in C# on .NET. It provides a SQL interface with a Raft-replicated, transactional key-value storage layer, and makes a few opinionated choices: **serializable isolation/strong consistency are the default**; databases can be **branched copy-on-write like code**; and **dropped objects are recoverable** instead of instantly destroyed. It can auto-scale based on traffic. Development is driven by performance, Jepsen-style testing, chaos engineering, fault injection, and degraded-state testing. ／ CamusDB's engine is written in modern C# on .NET: the SQL parser, the query planner and operators, the transaction layer, and the embedded Kahuna storage node all run in a single .NET process (with RocksDB underneath for persistence). Because the engine itself is pure .NET, extending it means writing ordinary C#: bring your own NuGet libraries and custom business logic directly into the database layer without crossing a language boundary or fighting a foreign extension API. Reading and debugging the engine is equally direct, and it runs on any platform .NET 10 supports. Clients talk to it over a JSON/HTTP API or a gRPC API with a .NET client library. ／ The same engine also compiles to WebAssembly and runs in a browser tab, with nothing to install: an in-memory node with a SQL editor and a sample data set. One button turns it into a three-node cluster inside that one tab, over an in-memory transport — stop the leader, watch another node take over, start the old one and watch it catch up. Try it at camusdb.github.io/playground. See docs/browser-playground.md to build it and serve it from any static host.
